definition: Craving, thirst, or desire — in the Buddhist tradition, the force that binds us to suffering by perpetually pulling us toward pleasant experiences and away from unpleasant ones.

used_in_sentence: He recognized the familiar taṇhā rising — the quiet, reflexive wanting that tells you the next thing will finally be enough.

definition: Impermanence. The characteristic of all conditioned phenomena constantly arising and passing away.
example: The thought came and went, anicca made plain — a cloud passing over the field of attention.
used_in_sentence: The thought came and went, anicca made plain — a cloud passing over the field of attention.

definition: The cessation of suffering; liberation. Literally 'blown out' or 'extinguished' — the quieting of the fires of craving, aversion, and delusion.
example: She did not talk about nirvāṇa; she simply sat in such a way that you forgot, for a while, that you had been looking for something.
used_in_sentence: She did not talk about nirvāṇa; she simply sat in such a way that you forgot, for a while, that you had been looking for something.

definition: Feeling-tone — the immediate, pre-verbal sense that an experience is pleasant, unpleasant, or neutral. In Buddhist psychology it is the hinge where craving is born, before thought ever gets involved.
example: Watch closely and you can catch the vedanā — the flicker of ‘pleasant’ or ‘unpleasant’ — that arrives a half-second before the wanting does.
used_in_sentence: Watch closely and you can catch the vedanā — the flicker of ‘pleasant’ or ‘unpleasant’ — that arrives a half-second before the wanting does.

definition: A mental impression or conditioned imprint left by past experience — the grooves of habit and reaction that shape how you meet the present moment, often without your noticing.

used_in_sentence: Every reaction you don’t question deepens the saṃskāra beneath it, until the groove is doing the choosing for you.

definition: Teaching, truth, or law — most often the teachings of the Buddha, and more broadly the way things actually are when seen clearly.
example: The dharma, one disciple said, is just this: that whatever arises also passes away.
used_in_sentence: The dharma, one disciple said, is just this: that whatever arises also passes away.

definition: Suffering, unsatisfactoriness, or existential dis-ease — the first of the Buddha's Four Noble Truths.

used_in_sentence: Even at the peak of the climb, dukkha waited, patient as weather.

definition: A fluctuation or modification of the mind — the ceaseless waves of thought, memory, and impression that ripple across awareness. Patañjali defines yoga itself as the stilling of these fluctuations.
example: Yoga, the sūtras say, is nothing more mystical than the settling of the vṛttis — the mind’s waters going quiet enough to see the bottom.
used_in_sentence: Yoga, the sūtras say, is nothing more mystical than the settling of the vṛttis — the mind’s waters going quiet enough to see the bottom.

definition: Non-self. The teaching that there is no permanent, unchanging self at the core of one's experience.
example: For a brief moment, the idea of anattā was not a concept but a relief — as if a weight he had been carrying without knowing had been set down.
used_in_sentence: For a brief moment, the idea of anattā was not a concept but a relief — as if a weight he had been carrying without knowing had been set down.

definition: Non-self — the recognition that no fixed, separate ‘I’ can be found at the center of experience. One of the three marks of existence alongside anicca and dukkha.
example: Look for the self anattā denies and you find only a procession of thoughts and sensations, with no one behind them holding the reins.
used_in_sentence: Look for the self anattā denies and you find only a procession of thoughts and sensations, with no one behind them holding the reins.

definition: Liberation from the cycle of birth and death; release into one's true nature.
example: The word mokṣa does not so much describe a destination as mark the moment the door swings open from the inside.
used_in_sentence: The word mokṣa does not so much describe a destination as mark the moment the door swings open from the inside.

definition: The ‘eight limbs’ of Patañjali’s yoga — yama, niyama, āsana, prāṇāyāma, pratyāhāra, dhāraṇā, dhyāna, and samādhi — a progressive path from ethical foundation to absorption.
example: The eight limbs of aṣṭāṅga are less a ladder than a spiral, each one quietly strengthening the others.
used_in_sentence: The eight limbs of aṣṭāṅga are less a ladder than a spiral, each one quietly strengthening the others.

definition: The five restraints — the ethical foundation of yoga and its first limb: ahiṃsā (non-harming), satya (truthfulness), asteya (non-stealing), brahmacarya (right use of energy), and aparigraha (non-grasping). How one relates to the world.
example: The yamas are the ground floor of the whole edifice; skip them and everything built above wobbles.
used_in_sentence: The yamas are the ground floor of the whole edifice; skip them and everything built above wobbles.

definition: The five observances — the second limb of yoga: śauca (purity), santoṣa (contentment), tapas (discipline), svādhyāya (self-study), and īśvara-praṇidhāna (surrender). How one relates to oneself.
example: If the yamas govern how you meet the world, the niyamas govern how you meet yourself.
used_in_sentence: If the yamas govern how you meet the world, the niyamas govern how you meet yourself.

definition: Non-harming — the first of the five yamas. Not merely refraining from violence but cultivating an active gentleness toward all beings, oneself included.

used_in_sentence: Ahiṃsā begins the moment you stop making an enemy of your own experience.

definition: Truthfulness — the second yama. Alignment between what is real, what one thinks, and what one says, so that word and world stop pulling in opposite directions.

used_in_sentence: Satya is expensive at first and free forever after; the cost is all paid up front, in the discomfort of honesty.

definition: Non-stealing — the third yama. Taking nothing that is not freely given, including time, energy, and credit, not just possessions.

used_in_sentence: Asteya asks a subtler question than ‘did you steal?’ — it asks whether you are living off what you have actually earned.

definition: Right use of vital energy — the fourth yama. Often translated as continence or moderation, it is the conservation and skillful direction of one’s life force rather than its heedless spending.

used_in_sentence: Brahmacarya is less about denial than aim — deciding, on purpose, where your energy is allowed to go.

definition: Non-grasping — the fifth yama. Holding life open-handed, taking only what is needed and clinging to none of it.

used_in_sentence: Aparigraha is the practice of enjoying a thing fully while already knowing how to let it go.

definition: Purity or cleanliness — the first niyama. Keeping body, environment, and mind clear enough that what is essential can be seen.
example: Śauca is the housekeeping of the soul: clear the clutter and the signal comes through.
used_in_sentence: Śauca is the housekeeping of the soul: clear the clutter and the signal comes through.

definition: Contentment — the second niyama. A settled sufficiency that does not depend on conditions improving, the antidote to the mind’s endless ‘not yet, not enough’.

used_in_sentence: Santoṣa is not resignation but relief — the quiet discovery that this, right here, was already enough.

definition: Disciplined heat — the third niyama. The willing friction of practice, the austerity that burns off impurity and forges the will, literally ‘to heat’.

used_in_sentence: Tapas is the heat you generate on purpose, the way effort held steadily becomes a kind of fire that refines.

definition: Self-study — the fourth niyama. The turning of attention back upon oneself, through sacred texts and through honest observation of one’s own patterns.

used_in_sentence: Svādhyāya is reading two books at once: the scripture in your hands and the self doing the reading.

definition: Surrender to the divine — the fifth niyama. The release of the small self’s grip and its offering up to something larger; the culmination of the observances.
example: Īśvara-praṇidhāna is where effort finally lays itself down, trusting the current it has been swimming against all along.
used_in_sentence: Īśvara-praṇidhāna is where effort finally lays itself down, trusting the current it has been swimming against all along.

definition: Cessation or stilling. In Patañjali’s definition of yoga — yogaś citta-vṛtti-nirodhaḥ — it is the quieting of the mind’s fluctuations that reveals what was always underneath.
example: Nirodhaḥ is not the suppression of the mind but its natural settling, the way a shaken glass of water clears when finally left alone.
used_in_sentence: Nirodhaḥ is not the suppression of the mind but its natural settling, the way a shaken glass of water clears when finally left alone.

definition: The sage traditionally credited with compiling the Yoga Sūtras, the foundational text that lays out the eight-limbed path (aṣṭāṅga) to liberation.
example: Patañjali’s genius was to take a sprawling oral tradition and compress it into a few terse lines you could carry in your pocket.
used_in_sentence: Patañjali’s genius was to take a sprawling oral tradition and compress it into a few terse lines you could carry in your pocket.

definition: Concentration — the sixth limb. The gathering of scattered attention onto a single point and the effort of keeping it there.

used_in_sentence: Dhāraṇā is attention learning to stay, returning to its object as many thousands of times as it wanders.

definition: Meditation — the seventh limb. The unbroken flow of attention toward its object, when concentration stops needing to be renewed.

used_in_sentence: Dhyāna begins the moment the effort of dhāraṇā dissolves and attention simply pours, uninterrupted.

definition: Absorption — the eighth and final limb. The collapse of the gap between observer and observed, where the meditator, meditation, and object become one.

used_in_sentence: In samādhi the watcher and the watched fall into each other, and for a moment there is no one left to be separate.

definition: Steady practice — the sustained, patient effort held over a long time, which together with vairāgya (non-attachment) stills the mind.

used_in_sentence: Abhyāsa is simply showing up again, and the power is not in any single sitting but in the unbroken chain of them.

definition: Non-attachment — the loosening of grasping and aversion that lets experience come and go freely. Paired with abhyāsa as the two wings of practice.

used_in_sentence: Vairāgya is the release valve to abhyāsa’s discipline: hold the practice tightly, hold its fruits loosely.

definition: Posture — the third limb. Originally a steady, comfortable seat for meditation; the body made quiet and stable enough to be forgotten.

used_in_sentence: Āsana is not the pose for its own sake but the stillness it buys — a body that will finally sit down and stop interrupting.

definition: Breath regulation — the fourth limb. The conscious extension and direction of the breath, and through it the life force (prāṇa) it carries.

used_in_sentence: In prāṇāyāma the breath becomes a handle on the nervous system, a lever most people never learn they are holding.

definition: Withdrawal of the senses — the fifth limb. The turning inward of attention, unhooking awareness from the pull of sights, sounds, and sensations.

used_in_sentence: Pratyāhāra is the sense-doors drawing closed, not by force but because something more interesting has appeared within.

definition: Life force — the vital energy animating all living things, carried on the breath and circulated through the body’s subtle channels.

used_in_sentence: Prāṇa is the difference between a body and a corpse, the current that a spiritual practice learns to gather rather than leak.

definition: The central channel — the subtle river of energy running along the spine from its base to the crown, through which awakened life force is said to rise.

used_in_sentence: When prāṇa stops scattering through the senses and gathers into the suṣumnā, the whole system turns to face inward.

definition: The coiled, dormant spiritual energy said to rest at the base of the spine, which awakens and ascends the central channel as practice deepens.

used_in_sentence: Kuṇḍalinī is described as a serpent asleep at the spine’s root, and its waking as the beginning of the return journey home.

definition: The cycle — the round of birth, death, and rebirth, and by extension the repetitive churn of craving and suffering the unawakened mind spins within.

used_in_sentence: Saṃsāra is not only lifetimes but afternoons: the same hungers and reactions circling back, dressed in new clothes.

definition: One liberated while still alive — a being who has realized freedom and yet remains embodied, walking the ordinary world unbound by it.

used_in_sentence: The jīvanmukta looks like anyone else in line for coffee; the difference is entirely on the inside.

definition: The landscape of non-dual perception — reality seen from the inside-out, no longer as a separate me looking at a separate you but as the one awareness remembering itself in everything it sees. In the book it is the territory one first visits only in glimpses, before body and mind can hold the door open.
example: This recontextualization is what the sages meant by the Kingdom — having viewed the glass from the inside-out.
used_in_sentence: This recontextualization is what the sages meant by the Kingdom — having viewed the glass from the inside-out.

definition: The reflection of God within creation — the divine light present inside the field of manifestation rather than beyond it. As Yogananda framed it, if God is an infinite sun of white light, the Christ is that same light shining within the world of form; in that sense every reflected spark of it is Christ.

used_in_sentence: The reflection of God within the field of manifestation rather than beyond it is the Christ.

definition: The transformed world the collective senses is incoming — not something uploaded or implanted by technology, but the flowering that awakening makes possible on the far side of civilizational upheaval. Not the goal of a personal project so much as its prerequisite.

used_in_sentence: Perhaps the New Earth, this very special place we all sense is incoming, is neither uploaded nor implanted.

definition: The book's final state: to be permanently throned in the Kingdom rather than merely visiting it — non-dual perception stabilized and the door held open for good. Named in the tradition as glorification and final liberation.

used_in_sentence: The final liberation. Bliss.

definition: The single, undivided awareness that looks out through every pair of eyes — that which looks, remembering itself in everything it sees. The one seer behind the appearance of many separate subjects.
example: A monad of that which looks, remembering itself in everything it sees.
